meta.title: Hebrew B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Hebrew → English (see the Hebrew, recall the meaning) and English → Hebrew (see an English meaning, recall the Hebrew). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1000 words for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise while travelling, to produce simple connected text on familiar topics, and to describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions, and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. The Hebrew taught is the modern standard language of Israel. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Hebrew, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 186 of the 1000 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — work, money and the economy, education, the news, media and technology, government, law and society, the environment and the weather, health and medicine, travel and transport, the household and its chores, relationships and the stages of life, feelings and character, religion and festivals, abstract nouns for ideas, reasons and plans, the connectors that join sentences, and the verbs of thinking, deciding, arguing and changing — and the other 814 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Hebrew, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word: every form of a noun or a verb added together, including the forms written with a prefix such as ו "and", ה "the" or ב "in" joined to the front. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed as Hebrew is normally written — without vowel points, in the full spelling — with the POINTED form beneath it, which shows how it is said, and Wiktionary's romanisation with the stress marked (shalóm, katáv). Words spelt alike are separate cards where the level teaches both (שֵׁם "name", שָׁם "there"). The Hebrew Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the letters and the vowel points. The 510 nouns show their gender and plural; the 315 verbs are given, as Hebrew dictionaries give them, in the past tense "he" form, with their infinitive, present, future and binyan (the verb pattern) beside them and, behind the All forms fold, their past, present, future and imperative by person. Real example sentences come with 997 of the 1000 words, three apiece for 983 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms, pointing and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
